1I OurBigBook.com
Euler's criterion states that for an odd prime number p and p∤a,
a(p−1)/2≡(pa​)(modp)​,
(1)
where the right-hand side is the Legendre symbol.
Let g be a primitive root modulo p. Its multiplicative order is p−1, so g(p−1)/2=1. This power has square gp−1=1, and the only roots of X2−1 modulo the odd prime p are ±1. Therefore
g(p−1)/2≡−1(modp).
(2)
Euler's criterion now gives (g/p)=−1, so every primitive root is a quadratic nonresidue.
Now let p=22k+1 be a Fermat prime, with k≥1. The number of primitive roots modulo p is
φ(p−1)=φ(22k)=22k−1=2p−1​.
(3)
There are also exactly (p−1)/2 quadratic nonresidues. Since every primitive root is a nonresidue, these equally large sets coincide. Thus every quadratic nonresidue modulo p is a primitive root, as summarized by Quadratic nonresidues modulo a Fermat prime.
Finally, p≡1(mod4) and p≡2(mod3). Quadratic reciprocity therefore gives
(p3​)=(3p​)=(32​)=−1.
(4)
Hence 3 is a quadratic nonresidue modulo p, and consequently
3 is a primitive root modulo every Fermat prime p with k≥1​.
(5)

The set K∩P is compact because K is closed and bounded, and the product
G(x)=∏j=1n​xj​
(6)
is continuous. By the extreme value theorem, G has a maximizer. Since K meets the interior of the nonnegative orthant P, some feasible product is positive, so every maximizer lies in IntP.
On IntP, maximizing G is equivalent to maximizing
F(x)=logG(x)=∑j=1n​logxj​.
(7)
The Hessian of F is
D2F(x)=diag(−x12​1​,…,−xn2​1​),
(8)
which is negative definite. Thus F is a strictly concave function, and it has at most one maximizer on the convex set K∩P. Denote this unique point by x∗.
For any x∈K∩P, the line segment
x(t)=(1−t)x∗+tx,0≤t<1,
(9)
lies in K∩IntP. Since F(x(t)) is maximal at t=0, its right derivative there is nonpositive:
0≥dtd​F(x(t))​t=0​=∑j=1n​xj∗​xj​−xj∗​​.
(10)
Therefore
j=1∑n​xj∗​xj​​≤n​.
(11)
This is the supporting inequality for the product maximizer on a compact convex subset of the positive orthant.
Suppose now that K is invariant under cyclic coordinate permutation. That permutation preserves the product, so uniqueness forces it to fix x∗. Hence
x∗=(r,…,r)
(12)
for some r>0. More explicitly,
r=x∈K∩Pmax​n1​j=1∑n​xj​​.
(13)
Indeed, cyclic symmetry averaging puts the diagonal point with coordinate equal to the mean of any x∈K back in K, while the preceding inequality with xj∗​=r gives ∑j​xj​≤nr.
Finally, given a=(a1​,…,an​)∈IntP, define
K={x∈P:∑j=1n​aj​xj​​≤n}.
(14)
This set is nonempty, closed, convex and bounded, and it contains a. By the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality,
∏j​aj​∏j​xj​​=∏j=1n​aj​xj​​≤(n1​∑j=1n​aj​xj​​)n≤1.
(15)
Equality holds only when all xj​/aj​ are equal and their sum is n, namely only at x=a. Thus this K has
x∗=a​.
(16)

For a binary block code, n is the common length of its codewords, m=∣C∣ is the number of codewords, and
d=minx,y∈Cx=y​​dH​(x,y)
(17)
is its minimum Hamming distance.
The parity extension is
C+={(x1​,…,xn​,∑j=1n​xj​):x∈C}.
(18)
Every extended word has even Hamming weight. The distance between two words increases by one exactly when their original distance is odd, so
C+ has parameters [n+1,m,d+],d+={d,d+1,​d even,d odd.​​
(19)

Words: 75 Articles: 1
3K OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 75
ii OurBigBook.com
Fix a coordinate, say the last one. The punctured code is
C−={(x1​,…,xn−1​):(x1​,…,xn​)∈C}.
(20)
Deleting one coordinate lowers each pairwise distance by at most one. Thus, when d≥2, no two words merge and
C− has parameters [n−1,m,d−],d−1≤d−≤d​.
(21)
In guaranteed-distance notation this is recorded as an [n−1,m,d−1] code. If d=1, puncturing a coordinate on which a distance-one pair differs can merge words, so its exact size must then be stated separately.

iii

Words: 171 Articles: 1
3K OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 171
iii OurBigBook.com
For a chosen coordinate and symbol ε∈{0,1}, the shortened code retains the words having that symbol in the chosen coordinate and then deletes that coordinate. For the last coordinate,
Cε​={(x1​,…,xn−1​):(x1​,…,xn−1​,ε)∈C}.
(22)
At least one of the two coordinate fibres contains at least ⌈m/2⌉ words. Choose that fibre and, if necessary, discard surplus words. Because all retained words agree in the deleted coordinate, their mutual distances do not change. Hence one can always obtain
C with guaranteed parameters [n−1,⌈m/2⌉,d]​.
(23)
Without discarding words, its size is that of the chosen fibre and its minimum distance is at least d.
For the final calculation, the given code is the whole space F23​, so its parity extension is the length-four even-weight binary code. In a binary symmetric channel, parity fails to notice a nonzero error exactly when an even number of bits flips. The possible error weights are therefore two and four. Their total probability is
(24​)p2(1−p)2+p4=6p2(1−p)2+p4​.
(24)
This excludes the weight-zero event, since it is not an undetected error.

4F OurBigBook.com
For the given effective enumeration of partial computable functions, the diagonal halting set is
K={n∈N:fn,1​(n) is defined}​.
(25)
A many-one reduction A≤m​B is a total computable function g:N→N such that
x∈A⟺g(x)∈B​.
(26)
The S-m-n theorem states that for every m,k≥1 there is a total computable function skm​ satisfying
fskm​(e,x1​,…,xm​),k​(y1​,…,yk​)=fe,m+k​(x1​,…,xm​,y1​,…,yk​)
(27)
whenever either side is defined.
Suppose first that X is recursively enumerable. Choose a program that halts exactly on inputs in X, and let e index a two-variable program that, on (x,y), ignores y and runs that program on x. By the S-m-n theorem,
g(x)=s11​(e,x)
(28)
is total computable and indexes the unary function
fg(x),1​(y)=fe,2​(x,y).
(29)
Therefore
x∈X⟺fg(x),1​(g(x)) is defined⟺g(x)∈K.
(30)
Thus X≤m​K.
Conversely, suppose X≤m​K through a total computable g. On input x, compute g(x) and simulate machine g(x) on its own code. This procedure halts exactly when g(x)∈K, equivalently exactly when x∈X. Hence X is recursively enumerable. We have proved the many-one completeness of the halting problem:
X is recursively enumerable⟺X≤m​K​.
(31)
Finally, use the stated fact that 0∈/K and define
S={0}∪{2n+1:n∈K}.
(32)
Then 0∈S∖K, so S=K. The total computable map n↦2n+1 satisfies
n∈K⟺2n+1∈S,
(33)
and therefore K≤m​S. This is a distinct representative of the halting many-one degree.

The per-capita net growth rate is the birth rate minus the death rate,
be−aN−d.
(41)
Multiplying by the population size gives the ordinary differential equation
dtdN​=N(be−aN−d)​.
(42)
This is the exponential density-dependent birth model.

Solution
Words: 54
ii OurBigBook.com
At a positive equilibrium, division by N gives
be−aN=d.
(43)
Since b>d, this has the positive solution
N∗=a1​logdb​​.
(44)
Write the vector field as F(N)=N(be−aN−d). Its derivative is
F′(N)=be−aN−d−abNe−aN.
(45)
At N=N∗, the first two terms cancel and be−aN∗=d, so
F′(N∗)=−adN∗<0.
(46)
The one-dimensional linear stability analysis therefore shows that N∗ is locally asymptotically stable.

The susceptible equation may be written
S˙=birth of susceptiblesbe−aSS​​−infectionβSI​​−natural deathdS​​.
(47)
The factor be−aS is a density-dependent per-capita birth rate. The law of mass action gives the infection incidence βSI, which transfers individuals out of the susceptible compartment.
Likewise,
I˙=new infectionsβSI​​−natural deathdI​​−disease-induced deathδI​​.
(48)
There is no birth term in the infective equation, so only susceptible individuals reproduce in this model. Infectives die at total per-capita rate d+δ. These terms define the susceptible-infective model with exponential density-dependent birth.

The disease-free equilibrium is (S,I)=(N∗,0). For
F(S,I)=S(be−aS−βI−d),G(S,I)=I(βS−d−δ),
(49)
the Jacobian matrix there is
J(N∗,0)=(−adN∗0​−βN∗βN∗−(d+δ)​).
(50)
Because this matrix is triangular, its eigenvalue are its diagonal entries:
−adN∗<0,βN∗−(d+δ).
(51)
The second eigenvalue is positive exactly when
N∗>βd+δ​​.
(52)
Under this condition the linear stability analysis gives an unstable disease-free equilibrium, agreeing with the epidemic invasion threshold.

At an endemic equilibrium, I∗>0. The equation I˙=0 then gives
S∗=βd+δ​​.
(53)
Since also S∗>0, the equation S˙=0 gives
βI∗+d=be−aS∗​,I∗=βbe−aS∗−d​.
(54)
This infective population is positive precisely when
S∗<a1​logdb​=N∗,
(55)
which is exactly the assumed instability condition for the disease-free equilibrium. Thus the endemic equilibrium of the susceptible-infective model with exponential birth exists.
At this equilibrium the relations above reduce the Jacobian matrix to
J(S∗,I∗)=(−aS∗be−aS∗βI∗​−βS∗0​).
(56)
Hence
trJ=−aS∗be−aS∗<0,detJ=β2S∗I∗>0.
(57)
By the trace-determinant stability criterion, both eigenvalues have negative real part. The linearization stability theorem therefore proves that the endemic equilibrium is locally asymptotically stable.

Consider the meromorphic function
f(z)=z(z2−1)eiz​.
(58)
Close the contour with a large semicircle in the upper half-plane, indenting above the three real pole −1,0,1. The large-arc integral vanishes by Jordan's lemma, while the upper-half-plane indentation rule gives
PV∫−∞∞​x(x2−1)eix​dx=iπ∑a∈{−1,0,1}​Res(f,a).
(59)
The three residue are
Res(f,−1)=2e−i​,Res(f,0)=−1,Res(f,1)=2ei​.
(60)
Their sum is cos1−1, so the residue theorem yields
PV∫−∞∞​x(x2−1)eix​dx=iπ(cos1−1).
(61)
The real part of the integrand is an odd function, so its full-line principal value is zero. Its imaginary part,
x(x2−1)sinx​,
(62)
is an even function. Taking imaginary parts and halving the full-line integral therefore gives
PV∫0∞​x(x2−1)sinx​dx=2π​(cos1−1)​.
(63)

The Euler--Lagrange equations for the quadratic Lagrangian are
mx¨+Vx=0.
(67)
For a normal mode x(t)=aeiωt, they become the generalized eigenvalue problem for small oscillations
Va=mω2a.
(68)
Put λ=mω2/k. With the stated spring constants,
kV​=(1+ε(1+δ)−ε​−ε1+ε(1−δ)​)=(1+ε)I+ε(δ−1​−1−δ​).
(69)

ν2−(1+δ2),

λ±​=1+ε±ε1+δ2​=1+ε(1±1+δ2​).

ω±2​=λ±​mk​,λ±​=1+ε(1±1+δ2​)​.

a OurBigBook.com
In the homogeneous background, v=0 and the physical velocity is the Hubble flow
u=aHx=a˙x.
(73)
The comoving coordinate x is held fixed by the time derivative in the fluid equation, so
∂t∂u​=a¨x.
(74)
Moreover, spatial homogeneity gives ∇Pˉ=0. The Euler equation therefore reduces to
ρˉ​aa¨x=−ρˉ​∇Φˉ,∇Φˉ=−aa¨x.
(75)
Taking the divergence in three spatial dimensions gives
∇2Φˉ=−3aa¨.
(76)
Consistency with the Poisson equation,
∇2Φˉ=c24πG​ρˉ​a2,
(77)
then requires
aa¨​=−3c24πG​ρˉ​​.
(78)
This is the pressureless, zero-cosmological-constant Raychaudhuri equation, obtained by the Newtonian fluid derivation of the Raychaudhuri equation.

b

Words: 82 Articles: 1
9B OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 82
b OurBigBook.com
The elementary Newtonian derivation of the Friedmann equation follows a test particle on the boundary of a finite expanding sphere. It therefore introduces a distinguished centre and can misleadingly suggest that all matter expands away from one origin.
The fluid derivation is local: the Euler equation and Poisson equation must be compatible in every comoving neighbourhood. It consequently describes a genuinely homogeneous infinite universe, in which every comoving observer sees the same Hubble flow, without selecting a physical centre. This is the improvement captured by the Newtonian fluid derivation of the Raychaudhuri equation.

The no-cloning theorem for two pure states states that, for distinct nonorthogonal states ∣c0​⟩ and ∣c1​⟩, there is no unitary operator U and fixed blank state ∣0⟩ such that
U(∣cj​⟩∣0⟩)=∣cj​⟩∣cj​⟩,j=0,1.

s=∣⟨c0​∣c1​⟩∣,0<s<1,

and suppose such a cloner existed. Applying it repeatedly would produce N copies. The inner product of the two possible N-copy states has magnitude sN, so their optimal success probability under the Helstrom-Holevo bound would be
PN​=21​(1+1−s2N​).
(90)
Already for N=2,
P2​>P1​=21​(1+1−s2​),
(91)
because 0<s<1 implies s4<s2. But cloning followed by the two-copy Helstrom measurement for two pure states would itself be a quantum procedure applied to the original single state, contradicting the optimal one-copy bound P1​. Hence the assumed unitary cloner cannot exist.
Equivalently, clone-assisted asymptotic state discrimination would give PN​→1, although two nonorthogonal states are not perfectly distinguishable. Thus the Helstrom--Holevo theorem implies the no-cloning theorem.

with 0log2​0=0. If the codeword c(μi​) has length si​, then its expected codeword length is

(94)
Define the probability distribution qi​=2−si​/K. By Gibbs inequality,

Since log2​K≤0,

Conversely, choose the integer lengths

Then 2−si​≤pi​, so their Kraft sum is at most one and the converse part of Kraft's inequality supplies a binary prefix code. Moreover,
E(S)=∑i​pi​⌈−log2​pi​⌉<∑i​pi​(−log2​pi​+1)=H(X)+1.
(98)
Thus the minimum expected length S∗ satisfies the Shannon noiseless coding theorem
H(X)≤S∗<H(X)+1​.
(99)
For a decipherable code with arbitrary lengths s1​,…,sN​, apply the lower bound to the uniform source pi​=1/N. Its entropy is log2​N and its expected length is (s1​+⋯+sN​)/N. Hence
Nlog2​N≤s1​+⋯+sN​​,
(100)
the total length lower bound for a decipherable binary code.
Now consider the cumulative construction. Since
bj​−bi​=∑k=ij−1​pk​≥pi​≥2−si​(j>i),
(101)
bi​ and bj​ cannot have the same first si​ binary digits: numbers sharing those digits lie in one half-open dyadic interval of length 2−si​. Also, pi​≥pj​ implies si​≤sj​. Therefore no earlier codeword bi∗​ is a prefix of a later one, and no later, weakly longer codeword can be a prefix of an earlier one. The cumulative Shannon code is thus a prefix code, hence decipherable.
An optimal code minimizes expected codeword length over all decipherable codes for the specified source probabilities. The cumulative construction need not be optimal. For example, if
(p1​,p2​)=(0.6,0.4),
(102)
then (s1​,s2​)=(1,2) and the construction gives codewords 0 and 10, with expected length 1.4. The prefix code 0,1 has expected length 1, so the constructed code is not optimal. In general, Huffman coding produces an optimal prefix code.

A partial recursive function is obtained from the three kinds of initial function of recursion theory—
the zero function, successor function, and projection function—by finitely many applications of function composition in recursion theory, primitive recursion, and unbounded minimization. Explicitly, primitive recursion has the form
f(x,0)=g(x),f(x,n+1)=h(x,n,f(x,n)),
(103)
while minimization takes the least y for which g(x,y)=0 and is undefined if no such y is found.
For the function in part (i), define
s(0)=1,s(n+1)=0.
(104)
The initial value 1=S(Z(0)) and the identically zero recursion step are primitive recursive, so this is a primitive-recursive definition of the required zero test. It uses no minimization.

Using the zero test s from part (i), define by primitive recursion
r(0)=0,r(n+1)=s(r(n)).
(105)
Since s(0)=1 and s(1)=0, the values alternate:
r(2k)=0,r(2k+1)=1.
(106)
Thus r is the required parity function and, like s, is primitive recursive without minimization.

iii

Words: 205 Articles: 1
12F OurBigBook.com

Solution

iii OurBigBook.com
Let g(n,k)=r(n), where r is the total primitive-recursive parity function from part (ii), and apply unbounded minimization in k:
p(n)=μk[g(n,k)=0].
(107)
If n is even, then g(n,0)=0 and p(n)=0. If n is odd, then g(n,k)=1 for every k, so the search never terminates and p(n) is undefined. Hence p is partial recursive. Because every function built without minimization is total, p cannot be defined without minimization; the functions s and r can.
It remains to characterize the functions built using only the initial functions and composition. They are exactly the functions
f(x1​,…,xk​)=corf(x1​,…,xk​)=xi​+c​
(108)
for some c∈N and some input coordinate i.
Indeed, the zero function is the first form, the successor function and each projection function have the second form, and composing functions of these forms preserves the classification: a constant outer function remains constant, while an outer function yj​+c selects one inner function and adds c. This proves necessity by structural induction. Conversely, applying the successor function c times to zero produces the constant c, and applying it c times to πik​ produces xi​+c.
Every function in this class is directly computable: an algorithm either writes the fixed constant c, or copies the ith input and performs c successor steps.

A set S is a deductively closed set of formulae when every consequence of S already belongs to it:
S⊢φ⟹φ∈S.
(153)
It is a consistent set of formulae when it does not prove a contradiction,
S⊬⊥.
(154)
If S is inconsistent, there is a formal derivation of ⊥ from assumptions in S. By the finite character of formal proofs, that derivation mentions only finitely many assumptions s1​,…,sm​∈S. Hence
{s1​,…,sm​}⊢⊥,
(155)
so this finite subset of S is already inconsistent.

If some Ti​ were inconsistent, it would prove every formula by the classical principle of explosion. Because Ti​ is a deductively closed set of formulae, it would then contain every formula and could have no proper extension. This contradicts Ti​⊊Ti+1​. Thus every Ti​ is consistent.
Let
T=⋃i=0∞​Ti​.
(159)
If T were inconsistent, the finite character of formal proofs would give a finite inconsistent subset R⊆T. The chain is increasing, so all finitely many members of R lie in some common TN​. Then TN​ would be inconsistent, a contradiction. Hence T is consistent.
If T⊢φ, a proof again uses only finitely many assumptions from T, all lying in some TN​. Thus
TN​⊢φ.
(160)
Since TN​ is deductively closed, φ∈TN​⊆T. Therefore T is deductively closed.
Finally, suppose that T were finitary. Part (b) would provide a finite R⊆T such that R⊢T. Choose N with R⊆TN​. Then TN​⊢T; since TN​ is deductively closed, this implies T⊆TN​. But
TN​⊊TN+1​⊆T,
(161)
a contradiction. Consequently T is not finitary, proving the increasing union of deductively closed sets.

A field extension L/K is a splitting field for f∈K[X] when f splits into linear factors over L and L is generated over K by the roots of f. Equivalently, it is the smallest extension inside an algebraic closure over which f splits.
To prove existence, choose an irreducible factor of f, adjoin one of its roots, and factor f over the resulting finite extension. If a nonlinear factor remains, adjoin one of its roots and repeat. Each step lowers the total degree of the unsplit factors, so after finitely many finite extensions the polynomial splits. The field generated by the roots obtained is therefore a splitting field.
The precise uniqueness theorem says that if L and L′ are splitting fields of the same polynomial f over K, then there is a field embedding isomorphism
φ:L⟶L′
(176)
whose restriction to K is the identity. More generally, an isomorphism of base fields carrying one polynomial to another extends to an isomorphism of their splitting fields. Thus splitting fields are unique up to base-field isomorphism; inside a fixed algebraic closure, the field generated by all the roots is literally unique. These facts are summarized by existence and uniqueness of splitting fields.

ω=αωα​;
(179)
minimality then forces it to equal Q(α,ω).

A representation is completely reducible, or semisimple, when it is a direct sum of irreducible representation. Equivalently, every invariant subspace has an invariant complement.
Maschke's theorem says that every finite-dimensional representation of a finite group G over a field of characteristic zero is completely reducible. More generally, it is enough that the field characteristic does not divide ∣G∣.
Schur lemma states the following.
  • If V and W are irreducible G-representations, every intertwining operator T:V→W is either zero or an isomorphism.
  • If V is finite-dimensional over an algebraically closed field, every G-endomorphism of V is a scalar multiple of the identity.
Indeed, kerT⊆V and imT⊆W are invariant subspaces. If T=0, irreducibility forces
kerT=0,imT=W,
(195)
so T is an isomorphism. For an endomorphism of a finite-dimensional complex representation, choose an eigenvalue λ of T. The intertwiner T−λI has nonzero kernel, so the first part forces
T−λI=0.
(196)
This proves the Proof of Schur lemma.
Now let ρ:G→GL(V) be faithful and irreducible over C. For every z∈Z(G), the operator ρ(z) commutes with every ρ(g). Schur's lemma therefore gives
ρ(z)=λz​I
(197)
for some λz​∈C×. Faithfulness makes z↦λz​ an embedding
Z(G)↪C×.
(198)
Since every finite subgroup of the multiplicative complex numbers is cyclic,
Z(G) is cyclic​.
(199)
This is the cyclic-center obstruction to a faithful irreducible representation.

such that r(y)=y for every y∈Y. A space is a contractible space if its identity map is homotopic to a constant map.

In particular, if that largest invariant subset consists only of x∗​, every trajectory in Ω approaches x∗​.

Thus every energy has its negative as an energy. The Coulomb Hamiltonian has arbitrarily large positive energies in its continuum, so this symmetry would force energies arbitrarily far below zero. It would have no lowest energy eigenvalue and therefore no stable ground state. This is the unitary time reversal reverses the energy spectrum obstruction.
Now let T be antiunitary. It is conjugate linear, so
T(i∣ψ⟩)=−iT∣ψ⟩.

(463)
The spectrum is preserved rather than reflected through zero, so the lower-bounded Coulomb spectrum and its stable ground state are compatible with time-reversal symmetry. This is why antiunitary time reversal preserves the energy spectrum.

This curvature component produces radial tidal acceleration: nearby freely falling particles separated radially are stretched relative to one another, while transverse separations are compressed. At the Earth, after removing the Earth's own field, the Sun and especially the Moon produce the familiar ocean tides known since antiquity.
There is no conflict with the equivalence principle. A freely falling local frame can remove the uniform gravitational acceleration at one event by setting the connection to zero there. Tides measure this spatial variation of gravity rather than gravity at a single point.

The geometry and boundary velocities are axisymmetric and linear in the axial pseudovector Ω. The pressure is a true scalar. No nonzero parity-even scalar can be formed linearly from Ω and the radial vector x: Ω⋅x is a pseudoscalar. Hence the flow-induced pressure is spatially constant.
Equivalently, taking the divergence of the Stokes momentum equation gives the Harmonic pressure and vorticity in Stokes flow result
∇2p=0,
(543)
and symmetry plus the homogeneous boundary data excludes every nonconstant harmonic pressure mode. Since pressure is defined up to an additive constant, we choose
p=0​.
(544)

At every radius, the pressure perturbation has the form
p​(r,t)=−ρ0​ωF(r)cosωt,
(576)
whereas the radial velocity is
ur​(r,t)=F′(r)sinωt.
(577)
Define the average over one forcing period T=2π/ω by
⟨Ir​⟩=T1​∫0T​p​(r,t)ur​(r,t)dt.
(578)
Then
⟨Ir​⟩=−ρ0​ωF(r)F′(r)T1​∫0T​cosωtsinωtdt=0​.
(579)
The same is true for the net flux through every concentric sphere.
Pressure and velocity are in temporal quadrature, so this is a reactive acoustic energy flux. The forcing establishes a standing wave in the closed, lossless annulus: compressional and kinetic energy exchange during each cycle, but no energy is transported outward on average. This is the pressure-forced standing acoustic wave in a spherical annulus.

Solution

Words: 119
c OurBigBook.com
At larger frequencies the denominator
D(α)=cosα+αsinα​
(580)
can vanish. Its zeros satisfy
tanα=−α
(581)
and are the normal-mode frequencies for a pressure node at the outer sphere and zero radial velocity at the inner sphere. Near one of these radial acoustic resonances, the ideal undamped harmonic response becomes very large; exactly at resonance the linear lossless initial-value problem develops secular growth rather than a bounded periodic solution.
In a physical system, fluid viscosity, thermal losses, acoustic radiation, and damping in the elastic shell keep the amplitude finite and shift its phase. A nonzero pressure-velocity phase component then supplies positive mean power. At sufficiently large amplitude the linear acoustic approximation can also fail, leading to nonlinear frequency shifts or shock formation.

Each QR decomposition Ak​=Qk​Rk​ gives
Ak+1​=Rk​Qk​=QkT​Ak​Qk​.
(582)
Induction therefore yields the first Accumulated QR factorization identity:
Ak+1​=Q​kT​AQ​k​​,Q​k​=Q0​Q1​⋯Qk​.
(583)
We next prove the corresponding factorization of a matrix power. The case k=0 is just A=Q0​R0​. If
Ak+1=Q​k​Rk​,Rk​=Rk​Rk−1​⋯R0​,
(584)
then the similarity formula above implies
AQ​k​=Q​k​Ak+1​.
(585)
Consequently,
Ak+2​=AQ​k​Rk​=Q​k​Ak+1​Rk​=Q​k​Qk+1​Rk+1​Rk​=Q​k+1​Rk+1​.​
(586)
The product Q​k​ is orthogonal, and the product Rk​ is upper triangular. Hence
Ak+1=Q​k​Rk​​
(587)
is a QR decomposition.

e1​=6​−2w1​+w2​+w3​​,e2​=3​w1​+w2​+w3​​.
(589)
The two displayed coefficient vectors are orthonormal and can be completed to an orthogonal matrix, so such a real symmetric matrix A exists. Every bi​ and ci​ is nonzero, but
b2​c3​−b3​c2​=0.
(590)
Indeed, with t=1/2​,
Ake1​−tAke2​
(591)
is a nonzero multiple of w1​, while the remaining direction in
span(Ake1​,Ake2​) is
vk​=2​w2​+(−1)kw3​​.
(592)
Thus
span(Ake1​,Ake2​)=span(w1​,vk​).
(593)
By the simultaneous iteration interpretation of the QR algorithm, the leading two columns of the accumulated Q factor span this same space. The leading block Bk​ is therefore an orthogonal-coordinate representation of the compression of A to this space. Since
w1T​Aw1​=1,vkT​Avk​=22+(−2)​=0,w1T​Avk​=0,
(594)
we have
Spec(Bk​)={0,1}
(595)

For completeness, the intended statement becomes true if one adds
Δ=bn−1​cn​−bn​cn−1​=0.
(596)
Let Zk​ consist of the first two columns of Q​k−1​. The Accumulated QR factorization identity gives
col(Zk​)=span(Ake1​,Ake2​).
(597)
After division by ∣λn​∣k, every component along
w1​,…,wn−2​ tends to zero because of the strict spectral gap, while Δ=0 makes the two surviving dominant components independent. Therefore these two-dimensional subspaces converge to the dominant invariant subspace
E=span(wn−1​,wn​).

There are two-by-two orthogonal matrices Uk​ such that
Zk​Uk​⟶W∗​=(wn−1​,wn​).

Bk​=ZkT​AZk​,
(600)

dH​(Spec(Bk​),{λn−1​,λn​})⟶0.​
